# The Armistice and the end of the First World War 

How did the First World War end? 

 Captain A W L Paget MC and Second Lieutenant P R J Barry MC of the 1st Battalion Irish Guards read news of the Armistice to their men at Maubeuge on 12 November 1918. All military operations had ceased the day before at 11am on 11 November 1918. © IWM (Q 3365) 

On 11 November 1918 Germany signed an armistice which ended the fighting between the Western Front.

An armistice is usually just a ceasefire. But the 1918 Armistice forced the Germans to leave occupied territory and to surrender weapons, aeroplanes and warships. 

In the autumn of 1918, Germany and its allies were exhausted. Their armies were defeated and their hungry citizens were beginning to rebel. 

As early as 29 September, German General and Strategist Erich Ludendorff decided that a cessation of hostilities must be sought. 

The need became more urgent as Germany’s allies began to drop out of the war.

The German government approached the United States with a request for an armistice. They hoped that this would be based on the 'Fourteen Points' laid down in January 1918 by US President Woodrow Wilson as a foundation for 'peace without victory'. 

With their troops bloodily engaged on the Western Front, American attitudes had hardened, and Wilson made it clear in October 1918 that Germany would have have to fulfil conditions including the end of unrestricted U-boat warfare and the removal of their current rulers for any settlement. 

After the Allies' Hundred Days Offensive further depleted Germany's military strength on the Western Front, a German delegation met with Allied Commander-in-Chief Ferdinand Foch on 7 November 1918, in a railway carriage north-east of Paris.

There the Armistice was drawn up and signed, with Foch ensuring its conditions would make it impossible for the German Army to recommence fighting. The terms demanded that German forces leave France and Belgium, surrender all military equipment (and U-boats) to the Allies, and form democratic government in Germany.

 Belgian girls with English, French and American troops during the Armistice celebrations in Belgium, 11 November 1918. IWM (Q 69031) 

On 9 November 1918, the final obstacle was overcome, when Kaiser Wilhelm II abdicated and fled into exile.

While a new Socialist government was formed, German Generals ultimately tarnished the new regime with the humiliation of the defeat, for which they themselves were responsible.

Armistice negotiations were finally agreed on 11 November 1918, with the guns falling silent at 11am.

The signing of the armistice was greeted with varied responses. In many Allied towns and cities - especially those freed from enemy occupation - there were scenes of happiness. However, the celebratory mood was tempered by the grief of the many thousands who mourned for the war dead.

Away from the Western Front, the signing of the armistice did not necessarily mean an end to conflict. Fighting continued while peace negotiations got under way.

## How was peace agreed after the First World War?

After the First World War ended, the critical business of shaping the peace began. Find out how peace was agreed after the war ended. 

 © IWM (Q 3365) 

On 11 November 1918, an armistice came into effect ending the war in Western Europe – but this did not mean the return of peace. The armistice was effectively a German surrender, as its conditions ended any possibility of Germany continuing the war. 

Although the armistice of November 1918 ended the war on the Western Front, the millions of men who were serving there didn't immediately return home. A demobilisation scheme was implemented, to ensure the gradual release of men from military service.

## What happened after the Armistice?

The end of the First World War did not mean an end to the fighting in many parts of Europe. Learn about what happened after the Armistice from November 1918 onwards.

 The arrival of the gun carriage bearing the Unknown Warrior at the Cenotaph, Whitehall, for the unveiling ceremony by King George V, 11 November 1920. IWM (Q 31513) 

While scenes of jubilation followed the Armistice, the scale of the loss and sacrifice endured by Britons during the First World War saw the need for commemorations to mark the national sense of grief.

Learn how the First World War is commemorated including the commissioning of the permanent Cenotaph in 1920, the establishment of permanent cemeteries by the Imperial (now Commonwealth) War Graves Commission, and the Hall of Remembrance.
